question: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician to discuss contraceptive options. She is currently sexually active with one male partner, and they have not been using any contraception. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. She is allergic to latex and copper. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following contraceptive methods is contraindicated in this patient?

enhanced_information: In this case, the 36-year-old woman has a significant smoking history of one pack daily for 15 years, which increases her risk of thromboembolic events. According to medical consensus, combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) are contraindicated in women over 35 who smoke more than 15 cigarettes per day due to the elevated risk of cardiovascular complications. The reasoning chains correctly identify that her smoking history makes COCs inappropriate. The other contraceptive options, including the diaphragm with spermicide, progestin-only pill, condoms, and intrauterine device (IUD), do not have the same contraindications based on her medical history and allergies. Therefore, the combined oral contraceptive pill is the only method contraindicated in this patient.
analysis: The core medical principle in this case revolves around the contraindications for combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) in women who smoke, particularly those over the age of 35. This patient is 36 years old and has a significant smoking history of one pack per day for 15 years, which places her at an increased risk for thromboembolic events. According to established medical guidelines, COCs are contraindicated in women who smoke more than 15 cigarettes per day due to the heightened risk of serious cardiovascular complications. The other contraceptive options presented (diaphragm with spermicide, progestin-only pill, condoms, and intrauterine device) do not carry the same level of risk and are considered safe for her to use. Therefore, the only contraceptive method that is contraindicated in this patient is the combined oral contraceptive pill. This reasoning aligns with the enhanced information provided, which supports the conclusion that COCs are inappropriate for her given her smoking status. Thus, the best-supported option is the combined oral contraceptive pill.
